questions.prompt: Walk through how HrisRules.ManagerChain validates one employee's proposed manager: where the visited set and the traversal start, how a cycle is detected, how the next manager is found and when the walk stops, why self-management fails at once, how a reference to an unknown manager is handled, and why the depth bound needs its own fixtures apart from cycle detection.

keyPoints.text: The visited set starts with the employee being validated.
keyPoints.quote: The visited set starts with the employee being validated.

keyPoints.text: The traversal begins at the proposed manager.
keyPoints.quote: The traversal begins at the proposed manager.

keyPoints.text: Each manager must be newly added; an identity already present means the chain returned to a visited node, which is a cycle.
keyPoints.quote: If an identity is already present, the chain has returned to the employee or another previously visited node and forms a cycle.

keyPoints.text: The dictionary supplies the next manager until a null root is reached.
keyPoints.quote: The dictionary supplies the next manager until a null root is reached.

keyPoints.text: Because the employee is already visited, self-management fails immediately.
keyPoints.quote: Starting with the employee already visited makes self-management fail immediately.

keyPoints.text: A manager identity missing from the supplied map is rejected.
keyPoints.quote: rejects references absent from the supplied map.

keyPoints.text: Depth is a separate rule: a long acyclic chain can still exceed the supported depth, so write separate fixtures.
keyPoints.quote: A long acyclic chain can still exceed the workshop's supported depth.

questions.prompt: Why does saving one employee's manager change validate every employee's chain rather than only the edited one? Use the root-with-descendants example, describe what the source builds and checks, name the kind of rule this is, and say when it would be acceptable to replace the whole-map check with an incremental algorithm.

keyPoints.text: Moving root R under another chain can push its deepest descendant past the depth limit even when R's own chain stays short.
keyPoints.quote: Moving R under another chain can make the deepest descendant exceed the supported depth even if R's own chain remains short enough.

keyPoints.text: Checking only the edited employee would miss that consequence.
keyPoints.quote: Checking only the edited employee would miss that consequence.

keyPoints.text: The save builds a map that includes the proposed relationship and runs ManagerChain on every entry before accepting.
keyPoints.quote: The source builds a map with the proposed relationship and validates every entry before accepting the change.

keyPoints.text: It is a global invariant enforced during a local edit.
keyPoints.quote: This is a global invariant enforced during a local edit.

keyPoints.text: The supported employee limit makes the whole-map check a deliberate bounded approach.
keyPoints.quote: The supported employee limit makes a whole-map check a deliberate bounded approach.

keyPoints.text: Only replace it once you can state which descendants must be revalidated and demonstrate equivalent behavior.
keyPoints.quote: Do not replace it with a clever incremental algorithm until you can state which affected descendants must be revalidated and demonstrate equivalent behavior.

questions.prompt: Why does a valid manager graph not settle who may be a manager or who approves PTO? Explain how existence and eligibility are checked separately on save and in PTO routing, and the surprising outcome that follows. Then explain why the org-chart route validates chains before rendering recursively, and how it detects that the employee set is over its bound.

keyPoints.text: ManagerChain only verifies that the referenced manager exists in its map.
keyPoints.quote: ManagerChain verifies that the referenced manager identity exists in its map.

keyPoints.text: The save separately checks the assigned manager is not terminated: existence does not imply eligibility.
keyPoints.quote: The save operation separately checks that an assigned manager is not terminated. Existence does not imply eligibility.

keyPoints.text: PTO routing does its own check for an active, manager-capable account and otherwise falls back to HR.
So an employee can have a non-terminated manager while a new PTO request routes straight to HR.
keyPoints.quote: An employee can have a non-terminated manager relationship while a new PTO request routes directly to HR because no eligible active manager account is available.

keyPoints.text: Graph validation comes before recursive rendering because a cycle could prevent termination or disconnect nodes.
keyPoints.quote: A cycle could otherwise prevent termination or leave nodes disconnected from the expected root structure.

keyPoints.text: Fetching one more than the maximum distinguishes an exactly full valid result from a truncated oversized one.
keyPoints.quote: This distinguishes an exactly full valid result from a truncated oversized dataset.

keyPoints.text: A plain Take(maximum) before rendering would hide the extra records.
keyPoints.quote: A simple Take(maximum) followed by rendering would hide additional records.
